title: The complete Linux name-resolution journey
summary: Typing a URL triggers far more than a DNS query. This lesson follows the exact path on Fedora: NSS, nsswitch.conf, /etc/hosts, resolv.conf, systemd-resolved, the recursive resolver, then TCP/TLS/HTTP.

sections.heading: Step 0: the application's own cache
sections.html:
The browser checks its internal DNS cache first. Many browsers also run their own resolver path: Chrome/Firefox may use DNS-over-HTTPS, in which case the query does not go through /etc/resolv.conf at all. This is why 'browsers cannot resolve but dig works' is a real, diagnosable situation: check about:networking#dns (Firefox) or chrome://net-internals/#dns, and check whether DoH is enabled.

Keep this distinction in mind for the whole lesson: the application decides which resolver path to use; the OS only provides one default path.

sections.heading: Step 1: NSS — the OS-level switchboard
sections.html:
On Linux, name resolution for ordinary programs goes through the GNU C Library's getaddrinfo() (and gethostbyname), which is implemented using NSS (Name Service Switch). NSS decides which sources to consult and in what order:

$ cat /etc/nsswitch.conf | grep -E '^hosts'hosts:      files mdns4_minimal [NOTFOUND=return] dns myhostname

Read that line left to right:

  • files — /etc/hosts.
  • mdns4_minimal — mDNS for .local names only (Avahi).
  • [NOTFOUND=return] — if mDNS says the name does not exist, stop rather than continuing to DNS.
  • dns — the DNS resolver module, which reads /etc/resolv.conf.
  • myhostname — resolves the local hostname.

Practical consequences: an entry in /etc/hosts wins over DNS by default, and a missing dns in that line breaks DNS for everything that uses NSS while leaving dig working — a classic 'the tool works, the app does not' trap.

sections.heading: Step 2: /etc/hosts
sections.html:
A tiny static table, checked before DNS. Correct uses: loopback entries, a few internal hosts on a lab machine, and temporary overrides during an incident. Wrong uses: maintaining real infrastructure (nobody knows it exists, it cannot be delegated, and every host needs its own copy).

127.0.0.1   localhost localhost.localdomain
::1         localhost localhost.localdomain
10.20.30.5  wiki.internal wiki

Because NSS consults it first, a stale hosts entry can make you chase a non-existent DNS problem for an hour. Always check it before blaming a resolver.

sections.heading: Step 3: which resolver is configured?
sections.html:
The dns NSS module reads /etc/resolv.conf:

$ cat /etc/resolv.confnameserver 127.0.0.53
options edns0 trust-ad
search corp.example.com

Three things to read from it:

  • nameserver — up to three; the resolver tries them in order with a timeout.
  • search — suffix list appended to unqualified names. ping wiki becomes wiki.corp.example.com. Multiple suffixes mean multiple queries, each able to fail differently.
  • options — ndots, timeout, attempts, rotate, and DNSSEC-related flags.

On a NetworkManager/desktop Fedora system, /etc/resolv.conf is often a symlink to a file NetworkManager generates, or to systemd-resolved's file. Both cases mean do not edit it by hand — the change will be overwritten. Change the connection's DNS settings instead.

sections.heading: Step 4: systemd-resolved and the stub at 127.0.0.53
sections.html:
127.0.0.53 is not a public server: it is a local stub listener owned by systemd-resolved. Identification first, always:

# is resolved actually running and is it the stub in use?systemctl is-active systemd-resolved
resolvectl status
# who owns port 53 locally?ss -lunp 'sport = :53'

If resolvectl status works and lists per-link DNS servers, resolved is in control. If it prints 'Failed to get global data: Unit dbus-org.freedesktop.resolve1.service not found', resolved is not in use and the nameservers in /etc/resolv.conf are being used directly by glibc.

Why this matters: with resolved, the per-link configuration can be split (VPN DNS for a VPN's domains, split-horizon views), and queries are cached twice — once in resolved, once in the upstream resolver. A DNSSEC validation failure inside resolved produces SERVFAIL that the upstream server never returned, which confuses people who only look at upstream logs.

Do not assume systemd-resolved is active. Fedora installations vary, and container/host images frequently use a plain resolv.conf. Verify before using resolvectl, and treat dig against a specific server as the ground truth for 'is the server answering?'.

sections.heading: Steps 5-8: the resolver answers
sections.html:
The query now reaches a recursive resolver (either the local stub, which forwards, or the configured nameserver directly):

  1. Cache lookup. If a valid cached answer exists (positive or negative) it is returned immediately, with the remaining TTL.
  2. Iteration. Otherwise: root -> TLD -> authoritative, following referrals.
  3. Authoritative answer. The authoritative server responds with the records, or NXDOMAIN if the name does not exist in the zone, or NOERROR/NODATA if the name exists but not with that type.
  4. Caching. The resolver stores the answer for its TTL (and a negative answer for the SOA's minimum).

Then the resolver returns the packet to the client, and NSS hands the address to the application, which finally calls connect().

sections.heading: Step 9: resolution is not a connection
sections.html:
This is the point most candidates blur. After DNS returns an address, an entirely separate chain runs:

StageWhat happensFailure looks like
Routing + ARP/NDPPick next hop, resolve its MAC'Network unreachable' / ARP never resolves
TCP handshakeSYN, SYN-ACK, ACK to port 443Timeout (filtered) or refused (no listener)
TLS handshakeCertificate check, key exchangeCertificate error, handshake failure
HTTPRequest/response4xx/5xx, redirect loop

A DNS failure gives an error before any packet leaves toward the server ("name or service not known"). A TCP failure gives a connection error after resolution succeeded. They are trivially distinguishable if you look at the error text and the timing.

checks.prompt: Browsers and curl cannot resolve names, but dig example.com works. What is the most likely cause?
options: NSS configuration or the resolver path used by the application differs — e.g. hosts entry, nsswitch missing dns, or the app uses DNS-over-HTTPS
checks.explanation: dig queries the resolver directly, bypassing NSS. If dig works and ordinary programs do not, the difference is in the application's resolution path: nsswitch, /etc/hosts, search domains or app-level DoH.

why_wrong.1: Expired records return NXDOMAIN for everyone, including dig.
why_wrong.3: dig would then also fail (or fall back to TCP).

checks.prompt: What does a name server of 127.0.0.53 in /etc/resolv.conf indicate?
options: The systemd-resolved stub resolver listening locally
checks.explanation: 127.0.0.53 is systemd-resolved's stub listener. It forwards to configured upstream servers and caches.

why_wrong.0: Root servers are public anycast addresses, not loopback.
why_wrong.1: It is valid; it is the resolved stub.

checks.prompt: Describe every step from typing a URL in a browser to the first HTTP request, naming the component responsible at each step and where caching can shortcut the path.

checklist.text: Browser DNS cache (and possibly browser DoH resolver) is consulted first.
OS resolution goes through NSS: /etc/nsswitch.conf decides files/hosts then dns.
The dns NSS module reads /etc/resolv.conf; on systemd-resolved systems 127.0.0.53 is the stub.
The recursive resolver answers from cache or iterates root -> TLD -> authoritative.
Answer cached for TTL and returned; NSS returns the address to the application.
Then a separate chain: route lookup, ARP/NDP, TCP handshake on 443, TLS handshake, HTTP request.
Any cache hit skips the corresponding part of the hierarchy walk.

checks.reference: Browser cache -> NSS (getaddrinfo) -> /etc/nsswitch.conf -> /etc/hosts -> resolv.conf nameserver (often the systemd-resolved stub at 127.0.0.53) -> recursive resolver cache -> iterative walk root/TLD/authoritative -> answer cached for the TTL -> returned through NSS to the application. Only after this does the transport chain begin: routing lookup, next-hop resolution with ARP/NDP, TCP SYN to port 443, TLS handshake, then HTTP. Caching at any level (browser, resolved, resolver) shortens or eliminates the hierarchy walk, which is why 'not every lookup resolves from the root' is the correct statement.

connect.title: Troubleshooting
connect.text: getent hosts and resolvectl test the OS path; dig tests the server. Knowing which you are testing is half the diagnosis.

connect.title: Case study 2 and 4
connect.text: One is a resolver problem, the other is 'DNS fine, transport broken'.

interview.q: What is the difference between /etc/hosts and DNS on Linux?
interview.a: /etc/hosts is a static local table consulted first via NSS (files before dns in nsswitch.conf). DNS is the distributed hierarchy queried through a configured resolver. hosts wins, which makes stale entries a common misdiagnosis.

interview.q: How do you prove whether DNS or the network is at fault?
interview.a: Resolve the name (dig/getent), then connect to the IP directly (ping, nc, curl --resolve). If resolution succeeds and the IP connection fails, it is transport or routing. If resolution fails, check hosts, resolv.conf, resolvectl and the server itself.
